title: Faustus disappoints (5.6–5.7)
hook: the famous teacher turns out charming but shallow
tomorrow: who was waiting at the end of the road to Milan?

segments.voice: Yesterday, loved in God: people change, but in God they stand firm. The line was love them in God.

The podcast host everyone quotes. Perfect pauses, warm laugh, an answer for everything. Then someone asks a hard follow-up. For years, Augustine had a voice like that waiting for him. Whenever he asked the Manichees, the group he had joined, a question they couldn't answer, they said: wait for Faustus. He'll explain everything. At last Faustus comes to Carthage. He's wonderful company. And he can't answer.
screen: `THE VOICE EVERYONE QUOTES.` → `WAIT FOR FAUSTUS.` → `WONDERFUL COMPANY. NO ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Augustine is fair to him. Faustus said what the others said, only more pleasantly. But what good is an elegant cup-bearer, he asks, to someone thirsty for a better drink? Then the line that turns the story: a thing isn't true because it's said well, and it isn't false because it's said clumsily. Wisdom and folly are like healthy and unhealthy food, and either one can be served on fine dishes or plain. So is a beautiful voice a trap, or a tool? Augustine himself argued both sides. The Confessions leans hard on the warning. Charm can carry an empty cup, and the listener who loves the music stops checking the drink. But elsewhere, in a handbook for Christian teachers, On Christian Doctrine, he made the other case. Falsehood uses every art of speaking, he says; why should truth stand there unarmed? Teach the truth, and teach it well. Both voices are Augustine's, and they don't cancel out. And Faustus has one more surprise. Augustine liked him better in the end. Faustus didn't bluff. He knew that he didn't know, and he wasn't ashamed to say so, a modesty Augustine calls more beautiful than the knowledge he'd hoped for.
screen: `AN ELEGANT CUP-BEARER.` · `NOT TRUE BECAUSE SAID WELL.` · `WHY SHOULD TRUTH STAND UNARMED?` · `HE KNEW THAT HE DIDN'T KNOW.` · then, large: `CHARMING, BUT.`

segments.voice: Bring back something you heard lately that sounded wonderful: a talk, a post, a pitch. Say out loud, in one plain sentence, what it actually claimed. Then sit with that sentence on its own, without the music, and see what's left in the cup.
Faustus disappoints. The famous teacher is charming and honest, but can't answer the questions, and Augustine learns that eloquent and true are different things.
The line to keep: charming, but, so look in the cup and not only at it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics read this chapter of the Confessions as a lesson in discernment: weighing what a teacher says, not only how well it's said. Augustine's On Christian Doctrine is still read by those who train preachers.
